# Appendix

#### Note S1. Financial-Inclusion Index Construction

The financial-inclusion index introduced in Section 2.3 and used as a matching covariate in Section 4.3 summarizes the non-credit dimensions of a farm household member's engagement with financial services. It is built on one record per household member, with that member's demographic characteristics averaged over the plots the member works, merged by enumeration area, household and member identifier to the harmonized financial-services release from which the indicators of Table S0 are drawn. The index is the first principal component of 14 indicators: the member's years of schooling, whether the member works in a financial institution, whether another member of the household does, whether the member owns an account with a financial institution or contributes to a savings scheme, and ten indicators of insurance cover (vehicle, medical, funeral, property, commercial, travel, life, retirement, education and other endowment or investment plans). The component is fitted on complete cases across all 14 indicators; on the current release the financial indicators are themselves complete, so that restriction binds only through years of schooling, which is carried down from the farmer file. Composite measures of this kind are standard in work that treats financial inclusion as a multidimensional construct spanning accounts, savings and insurance rather than as account ownership alone, in Africa as elsewhere [@Zins2016; @DemirgucKunt2017].

Three indicators available in the same release were deliberately left out: the community distances to the nearest bank, motorable road and public transport (Table S0). Coverage is the first reason. The community questionnaire is administered per enumeration area and does not reach every area, so the three distances are missing for about a fifth of the members in the release, and the complete-case rule would drop every one of them. That loss is not random. It falls disproportionately on urban enumeration areas in 2012/13, which is precisely the imbalance the harmonization avoids by joining the community block to the farmer records rather than restricting to it, so admitting the distances here would reintroduce the same selection one stage later. Construct is the second reason. The distances describe a place rather than a person and enter with the sign opposite to every other indicator, so a component that included them would mix how financially connected a member is with how far that member lives from a bank. Excluding them makes the index unambiguously the former and removes the need to reason about sign when the loadings are read.

Because the two rounds differ in the services they record and rural and urban localities differ in the services available, a component is fitted separately within each survey-round-by-locality stratum rather than once over the pooled data: on 8,083 members in rural GLSS6, 1,527 in urban GLSS6, 5,692 in rural GLSS7 and 971 in urban GLSS7, against 16,273 in the pooled fit that supplies the reference metric. The sign and the scale of a principal component are arbitrary, so the four stratum scores are not comparable as estimated. Each is therefore placed on the pooled component's metric by regressing the pooled score on the stratum score within the stratum and retaining the fitted values, a rescaling that fixes orientation as well as scale: where a stratum's component came out sign-flipped, the regression coefficient is negative and the fitted values still align with the pooled score. The strata are disjoint, so the rescaled scores coalesce into a single value for every member. Three variables are released. `FinIdx` is the rescaled component itself. `FinIdxSi` is `FinIdx` min-max scaled over the pooled sample to the unit interval, and it is the variable that enters the matching distance of Section 4.3. `FinIdxCat` is the weighted quintiles of `FinIdx`, also taken over the pooled sample. Both transformations are pooled rather than within-round, so they express a member's absolute position on the index and not a rank within a survey round; and because the scaling is min-max, `FinIdxSi` is by construction sensitive to a single extreme value, which compresses the remaining members into a narrower band than a rank or quantile transform would.

Table S6 reports the first-component loadings and the share of variance the component explains in each stratum, and they warrant a careful reading rather than a reassuring one. In the pooled fit every loading is positive and the two largest are on years of schooling and on account ownership, followed by life and vehicle insurance and by financial-sector employment, so the pooled metric is oriented in the direction the index's name implies and the rescaling carries that orientation into every stratum. Two departures qualify this. Travel insurance has no variation in either 2016/17 stratum and is screened out of both, so the index rests on 14 indicators in 2012/13 and on 13 in 2016/17; taken with the fact that account ownership captures mobile money only in the later round, the index's content is not identical across the two rounds. And one loading is negative: commercial insurance in the urban 2016/17 stratum. It is near enough to zero to carry little weight in the score, but a mixed sign pattern is the signal that a first component is picking up something other than inclusion, and it is reported here rather than smoothed over. The more consequential diagnostic is the explained variance. The first component accounts for about a seventh of the variance in a set of 14 indicators, where a component carrying no information at all would account for about a fourteenth. The component is therefore informative but far from dominant: the indicators it summarizes are only loosely correlated with one another, a single dimension does not come close to exhausting them, and a different indicator set or a different scaling would produce a different ordering of members. This is the substantiation of the limitation that Section 6 states, and it is the reason the index is used to balance a comparison rather than to carry an interpretation.

What the index is not, finally, is the treatment. The treatment throughout this paper is `credit_hh`, the household credit indicator defined in Section 2.2 and documented in Table S0. The index enters in two other roles: `FinIdxSi` is one covariate in the distance on which each credit-using household is paired with a non-user, so that borrowers are compared with non-borrowers of similar overall engagement with financial services (Section 4.3), and `FinIdxCat` is available in the estimation as a dimension of heterogeneity. No exhibit in this paper reports results by the index's quintiles; heterogeneity across financial services is examined on the observed indicators themselves, formal account ownership above all (Figure 2 and Table 6). The index is estimated on 16,273 household-member records, a larger set than the `r fmt_num(objs$sample$n_pooled, 0)` farm operators of the analysis sample, so index values exist for records the frontier analysis does not use; the matching draws on the values it needs and discards the rest.

| `RePaid` | s12aq13 | s12aq13 | Amount of loan repaid (including charges etc.) | Continuous, cedis; deflated to 2016/17 prices |
| `credit_self` | derived | derived | Applied, granted, and a positive amount recorded | 0, 1 |
| **`credit_hh`** (treatment) | derived | derived | `credit_self` for the operator, spouse, a child, or any other household member | 0, 1 |
| `credit_spouse` | derived | derived | `credit_self` for the spouse, via the roster link | 0, 1 |
| `credit_child` | derived | derived | `credit_self` for a child, via the maternal and paternal roster links | 0, 1 |

| Reason for not applying | s12aq15 | s12aq15 | What was the main reason for not trying to obtain a loan? | 1 No need, 2 Interest rate too high, 3 Demand for collateral, 4 Already has too much debt, 5 Cannot obtain the amount needed, 6 Other |

| `BankKm`, `RoadKm`, `TrnprtKm` | community module | community module | Distance to the nearest bank, motorable road, and public transport | Continuous, km; minimum within the enumeration area |

*Notes*: Items are drawn from Part B, Section 12a of each questionnaire
(`sec12a` in GLSS6, `g7sec12a` in GLSS7); GLSS7 suffixes multi-response items
with `_a`, `_b` and so on, which the harmonization strips. Wording is
reproduced from the survey instruments. Loan detail is elicited only from
respondents who applied and were granted a loan, so the credit indicator is the
conjunction of application, approval and a positive amount rather than a test on
the amount alone. Mobile money and susu accounts do not appear in the GLSS6
instrument, so their zero entries in Table 2 denote items not asked rather than
an absence of holdings; the GLSS6 columns for the remaining institution and
account items are re-indexed onto the GLSS7 positions before the rounds are
pooled. GLSS7 records the status, source, purpose and collateral of up to three
loans but a single loan amount, and adds a "processing" outcome that GLSS6 does
not offer. The source-of-knowledge item is reported in Table 2 but is not
discussed in the text; its derived category indicators do not currently
reproduce the response order shown above, and the block is withheld from the
narrative pending correction. Distances are taken from the community
questionnaire rather than from Section 12a.
